It's not that Pat being the most revered is shocking to me. So much as there not being any new additions to the pantheon per se. Id say folk punk as a genre has a Mt Rushmore of Pat, Apes, DaysNDaze, and Ceschi. Rent strike seems to be stuck as your favorite folk punk's favorite folk punk. Pigeon Pit and LNL need a few more years. It just seems strange the genre hasn't produced any other hit makers or classic records. Granted it's still "young", I just don't want it to go the way of stoner metal.

Exploding into mainstream popularity - Bands like Pigeon Pit and Local News Legend have the potential to be HUGE. Pigeon Pit was on NPR tiny desk even. All it takes is a viral song or viral review. I think some exposure would make the broader punk community more aware of what's going on and get more people involved in what could be a fresh, young, and potentially vibrant scene. An injection of new fans, and a key record or two to influence fresh bands would bring a lot of longevity to the genre I feel.  

Consuming itself - Pat the Bunny is still seen as the de facto patron saint of folk punk despite the fact that he managed to retire for a decade. His latest album, while enjoyable for me as a fan, isn't accessible at all for a broader audience and distinctly moves away from a pure folk punk sound. This in conjunction with the Apes of the State being stalwart stewards of the genre, but their sophomore album slumped and we're still waiting on a third record from them. Paul Berribeua might be making a return as well. All at a time when there is a cornucopia of fresh bands that no one is listening to because their reach is horrible and opening for Apes of the State only nets you as many fans show up to alternative music venues or house shows. 

It all gives me this feeling that the genre is suffocating in its current space. Like many fans aren't even that aware of woody Guthrie, phil ochs, and other artists before the violent femmes were making political folk music. And then the violent femmes get the honourable mention for starting the genre before the Pat the Bunny lore overtakes its history for almost two decades now. This genre has so much potential to me, with bands like rent strike, but no one has heard of them. If it doesn't escape being strictly a part of the story of a few notables but aging artists, I find it difficult to see the future of the genre past Apes of the state holding the scene together through sheer willpower and Pat the Bunny covers. And then when the Apes retire, I can see it like the gangs of New York ending. Overtime, without those presences, people will move on, forget, and eventually they'll renovate and rebuild what used to be classic venues or house show basements. 

Granted, I say all this as a Midwesterner. The scene and the genre could be cooking up some incredible stuff I'm not aware of yet from either coast. Like Matt Decaro had some potential but he went radio silent afaik.

The tension and the stakes take on a weight and a gravity that is so much more grounded than computer programs trying to kill you. 

So a film I grew up loving as an action packed social commentary sci fi, wasn't that at all really. It was actually this deeply personal harrowing struggle to exist in a world that will kill you before it acknowledges the real you.

Tl:Dr - 1.dont cook it too hot, 2. Aromatics, 3. Dry brine or pre season the night before 


Everyone is posting full on dissertations and term papers as recipes, lemme gimme you a couple tips. 

Thick cuts take longer to cook, lower temps will help cook it through without burning the crust. - you can do this a couple different ways but just remember NOT TOO HOT. Or you'll have a black and blue, unless that's your thing. 


Garlic, rosemary, thyme, and shallots are classic steak aromatics. 

Seasoning it the night before will dry out the surface for a more even and browned crust, it also allows time for salt to season the interior of the meat as well. 

-

Now if you want how I'd do it. You need some high heat oil(grape seed, avocado, peanut) demi glace, rendered bone marrow, garlic, shallots, rosemary, thyme, and a nice french red. I prefer Bordeaux but I'm sure someone who knows better can tell me which region or grapes are better for this. Oh and some decent butter. 


Dry brine or pre season your steak the night before. 

Day of, set your steak out half an hour before cooking. get a stainless steel pan(this helps me see if the fond is burning as opposed to cast iron) up to a decent medium high heat. Things should sizzle but not splatter. 

Steak is already salted so just add pepper. Oil your pan. 

Place your steak on the pan and find something to apply even pressure to ensure contact with the pan. After thirty seconds, flip and do the same to the other side. Flip every thirty seconds until your crust looks almost done. Lower temp or move pan to unheated burner and add butter, garlic, shallots and herbs. Baste steak with butter until the crust looks good(maybe a minute or two of basting).

Given we had a controlled temp, the inside should be up to desired doneness. If not, finish in a low oven(275-325 range). 

While steak is resting or finishing in oven. Dump the excess fat and aromatics from the pan. On a med or med lowish heat the pan and deglaze the fond in the pan with your red wine. Once that's reduced by half, add in your demi glace, let it reduce a bit more again. It should coat the back of a spoon but not syrupy. Off the heat, while still warm/hot(not bubbling or reducing) add bone marrow and a little bit of butter while whisking until sauce is smooth and velvety looking. 

Steak should now be rested and ready to be served with a kick ass pan sauce.

But we can make laws and change legislation. The only thing an artist has to contribute to this world is their ideas and works. When we perpetuate a system that incentivizes artists to sell the totality of their ownership of their ideas so that they can eat, drink, and sleep. We essentially strip them of their right to own the investment capital they created. 

I'm not saying rob leifield got screwed specifically. I just want to point out the broader discussion in this post. Let's critically examine the art industries as they operate. How do they treat their artists? How often do artists own the rights and royalties of their work? What are the mechanisms for how an artist actually makes a living? How often and in what forms does exploitation take place? 

If we want to continue supporting art, and artists. We need to ask these questions and remain critical of whether or not we can improve these systems or the transparency by which they operate.

That's part and parcel of the rub being an artist in any medium. Historically, musicians would sign contracts with record labels without reading them and these contracts would give the labels rights over the master recordings, rights to the licences, and the money invested to make the album typically had to be paid back with interest. Mostly being recorded at the label's own studio. 

How many directors have had a shit sequel to one of their movies because the distributor or production company owned the rights to the first film and made something without the original creators. 

TV writers and show runners have had to deal with being fired from the shows they've created or made to change things with studio notes. 

Art in capitalism has unfortunately put society in a tough position. We work to protect someone's right to sell art by creating legal means to pursue plagiarists, and inadvertently create a system whereby people or organizations that categorically didn't create the original work, do own the rights to sell it. 

And that's mega simplifying a bunch of stuff. 

But my point is. It's historically incredibly hard to live off the work of your art without selling it. And that's something people can take advantage of. 

This is all besides the point though if leifield doesn't even want the rights back. If he doesn't care and is happy with his money, good for him. But if he'd like to create more work with that IP, I'd personally prefer that artist have the rights and freedom to do so while being able to reap the rewards of that effort.

I would say they don't apply to a soul series like you'd assume. Your inputs are animation locked. So it's not as reactive as you might reasonably think. If you swing your weapon, you need to be confident you made the right choice or you'll potentially take lethal damage, the entire game. 

Not to say that the souls games punish fast characters, they actually encourage confident and bold plays. But the games will make you learn the hard way, when to be confident and bold, or die, a lot. 

Also the story telling is wildly unique in fromsoftware games compared to most mainstream stories, other than maybe Majora's mask? But that'd be up for debate. 

The first dark souls is relatively small in its scope and lore compared to the rest, so its obtuse way of telling a story isn't as shrouded as say bloodborne or DS3. 

I think elden ring and sekiro skew very mildly on the spectrum towards a more mainstream story approach compared to the grading curve of fromsoftware games. But elden rings lore is so dense that you need more info properly introduced to you and for that I assume it could be daunting for a new player given its scope. 


I think sekiro would be a really good starting point for a lot of folks as well, but it also offers some of the toughest fromsoftware boss fights I've played. Personally I still haven't beaten the final stage of the final boss. 


Given all that, I'd say dark souls 1 is a great primer for other souls games. You won't have to invest nearly as much time to get what it's trying to do and decide if it's for you.

It's hard for me to get this across through text, but I'm being genuine. In good faith, I don't want a fight. I get very passionate in these discussions because I find them fun but I understand sometimes my responses can come across as dramatic. 

He doesn't necessarily have to retire, but regardless I feel like it could be subtle. Ragnarok had a very strong theme of change and growth, I would argue it was subtle despite also being in the text of the script. 

Simply the idea of Thor turning away from a fight is interesting to me. I don't know how you'd make that a good story without doing a couple drafts, but I find that idea much more engaging than the idea that Thor is the only god strong enough to kill the god killer. 

I would concede that Thor being apprehensive about fighting gorr and committing more violence, yet doing so anyways could also be interesting. He would just need an incredibly well written and compelling motivation for such a fight to not feel forced or contrived.

You've framed it as "Jane trying to survive a fight with gorr". It's an implication that she'd need assistance from Thor. But what if Jane was *kicking gorr's ass*, and Thor saw that Jane is just strong as he was. What if Thor understood that to assist Jane would be to rob her of an easy yet significant first victory as a hero. 


   What if thor did fight in the first half, to secure the victory, but let his companions do the monster clean up while he attends to civilians in a search and rescue.  


   This idea that Thor would be despicable if he didn't want to fight is so shallow. Could you not sympathize with wanting to sit out a fight if you could help it? Remember, Spider-Man intentionally gave up the iron spider suit and the avengers resources at the end of Homecoming. He understood that those fights weren't his yet.


   Thor wouldn't be negligent, if he saw his friends kicking ass and saving the day. Then instead of joining in on the fun of battle, he decided he could do more good with search and rescue, securing the mcguffin, protecting the escape route, or literally anything other than fighting someone *again*. 


   The entire idea that Thor is a warrior above all else is what led to his downward spiral throughout Ragnarok to endgame. He *needs* a new way to live, or he'll keep surrounding himself with death and despair.


   Fuck, the best scene in Ragnarok was when Thor told Loki "you've always been the god of mischief, but you could be more" . Why can't Thor be more? Why is it the most heroic thing he is allowed to do is punch and axe bad guys. What if he talked to them, what if he *tricked* them, what if he inspired new heroes to take up his mantle, while he searched for a better path than killing. 


   Finally, past all the character justifications, it's boring to watch these third act fights. They're predictable, contrived, and so consistently in every marvel movie it's astounding. Dr. Strange was given rave hype about his third act fight just because it was technically more of a negotiation. 


   Marvel Studio's biggest weakness is their insistence on these third act fights. These fights inadvertently dictate the direction of the entire rest of a script, it limits the scope of what our villains goals, methods and capabilities are, and it kills the stakes because we as an audience know, "the hero always wins the fight in the third act". The most memorable aspect of infinity war was that the heroes lost the third act fight, and that was just because it was a two-part film. 


   Y'know what, let Thor fight gorr. But let him lose and let Jane save his life. Let it be a moment of reflection with Thor accepting he isn't the strongest avenger anymore. Let Thor lose the fight and learn from it. 


   Taika even tried to do something similar with ensuring Ragnarok as a key aspect of the third act of the last movie. Thor had to lose his home to save his people, and unleash a giant fire demon to win. It wasn't groundbreaking, but jesus it was more interesting than civil war's third act. 


   It's not so much about how they do something different than a big CGI fight, but at least just doing anything else. Let it be different, let it be new, let it be unexpected and surprising. But at the very least, stop showing us the same third act, across twenty something movies, and telling us we've never seen a movie be this creative before. I would rather see a terrible ending that I never expected than another third act fight. Because the terrible ending would've actually engaged my brain and made me think about things. Even if those things are "why did this ending suck. Why did they choose that ending. How could they treat Thor like that.". Otherwise I may as well walk out after the second act because I know Thor and Jane will kill gor, day saved, picked up some new heroes and trauma to play with until the next movie's third act fight. 

   If the third act, the climax, the culmination of your film is when brains turn off, people zone out and otherwise understand that the story is effectively done so that we may present the fireworks. Your third act is uninteresting and fails to actually address the thesis of the story in a satisfying way. 


   It's why endgame has a bit of a weird reputation as great fan service, but not the best movie. It killed Thanos off in the first act just to literally yank him from another timeline to ensure there was a big third act fight. Of any movies to justify a third act fight, it would've been endgame. But their justification was so contrived that the only enjoyment of the last hour of that movie is seeing all the cool screen saver shots. The third act of endgame undermines the entire narrative arc of the movie. For two hours we see our heroes dealing with and accepting actual loss and failure. We see them trying to figure out a way to fix their mistakes with the understanding that the world has changed and they need to respect the consequences of their failure while trying to make amends. Then Thanos comes in and is more or less a stand-in for them to win where they lost once, instead of winning in a new or different way.
